So that is a different context as well. So for example, we took an image of a church building from Wikipedia, and we artificially embedded it in an article for building material for ~ Churches, I believe, and the third one. We didn't say take care, like of the type of context that this image appears in or But we simply presented that image within a different Wikipedia article in each case. And what we found is that the type of descriptions that people then wrote for those images changed. And when we then tried to evaluate those descriptions with fully sighted participants and with blind and low vision participants, in order to get the quality of those descriptions, we found that both sighted participants and then blind and low vision participants were highly affected by. How much the description was made relevant to that particular article. So when you have an image like of a church and in an article on building material, then participants really wanted to know about what the building material looked like, right? So we can keep coming up with scenarios where no default description would ever include that type of information, making the point that this context of how we approach that image really, really matters for making descriptions that are actually useful. I'm saying no one, which is an exaggeration, but really a large majority of that work never work with blind and low vision users to investigate actual preferences. the communities that they should serve. For the blind and low vision community, for example. And so a lot of work in human-computer interaction, and what I also try to show in my work, are where these two actually come apart.

they definitely communicated a lot of discontent when it wasn't apparent why that image was there in the first place. and some automatic metrics that should be able to capture that relation. So I'm interested in your opinion about the metrics that were available at the point of you doing that work. Did you find any metric that you found useful? at that time and if yes, what was it, if not, how you dealt with that. Yeah, that's a very good question. So one of the core cornerstones of my research is basically that evaluation is incredibly important and doing it well is really difficult.

And often evaluation is done by thinking that evaluation is easy and straightforward, and that can introduce some very problematic artifacts. And so When we're talking about image description evaluation, for example, that is usually done by just taking that image out of context and then taking that description that we have as a candidate and asking, is this description good for this image? Right? And as you can tell, this is taking the image out of context, right? So even if you give that to people, and these are the most well-intended people in the world. If you don't give them the context, there's no way that they could judge it, right? So this is the onus is on us as researchers, on us as evaluation designers to first understand what are all the different variables that are important in the first place in order to get an evaluation that then actually makes sense.

So, and this is an issue not just when we're running human subject studies, but often in AI research, or usually always, ~ We want metrics that where we don't have to ask people all the time, right? Because it's not scalable. So instead, we want some type of automatic metrics that can, to a reasonable degree, approximate what people would say. So that when we make small adjustments to the model, to the data, whatever it may be, we can already get some suggestion on whether we're moving into the right direction. Now, in that same vein, a lot of the metrics that have been designed have been designed in order to keep basically this compatibility between the image and the description in mind.

So the most prominent one of those is CLIPScore, which is still used a lot today, where the idea is that ~ I have a lot of different pairs of images and descriptions from the internet that belong to each other. And now when I just shuffle them, then I have contrastive pairs where I know that they don't belong together. And so I can train a model to basically be able to tell do these two go together or do these two not go together. So I like to think of it as a type of compatibility metric. Like, is that description compatible with this particular image or not? And for that, it's a really amazing tool. Like it's very fantastic, it does the job really well. But people are also using it a lot in order to estimate quality of a description.

But in the way that I just explained to you how this metric works, it doesn't take context into account at all. And so basically, in this work, we tested to what extent that matters. And what we find is that it very much matters, that as soon as you give people the opportunity to judge the quality of a description based on the context that image was in the first place, we cannot replicate any correlation with the CLIPScore ratings at all anymore, because people really care about how relevant it is to a context. And you lose all of that if you use metrics like CLIPScore that completely extract the context away. And since we're always working in contextual scenarios, that is something that should be very concerning to us when we keep optimizing systems and we use metrics that are steering it in directions that are not necessarily helpful.

So My bottom line when you're asking, you know, what metrics do I like, we had some other work where we tested vision language models more at large, whether they can be used as judges for image description evaluation when you include context and so on. And so far I haven't Come across a metric that I would fully trust in all of those regards, because we also find that everything that we've tested so far has certain types of biases that can always stir models in undesirable directions. So even though there are good proxies for different things that you would want to do, so for example, we find that metrics like CLIPScore that are more Operating on embedding space, they are really good for truthfulness evaluation and compatibility. For that, use those metrics.

Excellent. Don't use the VLMS judges. Hallucinations are way more obvious there. When it comes to contextual sensitivity, do not use the embedding based metrics. But overall, the best thing and the most important thing that we need to do at some point is actually testing it with people and doing that well. So that would be my plea.
